title: Canary Traffic Orthogonalization — Lab Notes & Blend Patterns
content:
Purpose and scope:

This note collects exploratory patterns and pragmatic checklists for running cross-functional canaries and A/B experiments at Redwood where multiple axes of change (model variant, quantization, routing policy, batch tuning) must be tested simultaneously without contaminating overlapping cohorts. The tone is lab-notes: sketches, failed attempts, heuristics that worked in staging, and open questions for the rollout guild. Not a final playbook.

Why orthogonalization matters here:
- Many of our features affect both cost and quality (e.g., 4-bit quant vs fp16). If cohorts are not orthogonalized, a product-level metric drop could be misattributed.
- Multi-dimensional changes (model + routing) increase the combinatorial space; we need strategies to separate signal.
- Rapid progressive rollouts must preserve SLOs while allowing informative experiments with minimal blast radius.

Core definitions used in notes:
- Orthogonal cohort: a cohort partitioned to hold only one independent variable (primary axis) while other variables remain controlled.
- Blend: proportionally mixing traffic between a baseline and multiple variants within a single route for runtime experimentation.
- Dynamic allocation: continuous traffic rebalancing driven by a reward/penalty signal (not the same as full MAB production control; used conservatively).

High-level patterns (sketches):
1) Nested one-factor-at-a-time canary (recommended default)
   - Split traffic into baseline (85%), primary canary (10%), safety-slice (5%).
   - Primary canary changes only one axis (e.g., model version).
   - Safety-slice receives the most conservative fallback paths (e.g., same model with stricter timeout) and is observed for worst-case regressions.
   - Rationale: reduces confounding; easy rollback.

2) Orthogonal matrix slices for parallel experiments (when you must test 2 axes concurrently)
   - Create 4 cohorts (A: baseline, B: model-change-only, C: routing-change-only, D: both changes).
   - Keep cohort sizes small (2–7% each for B/C/D depending on risk appetite).
   - Use pairwise comparisons (B vs A, C vs A, D vs B/C) to infer interactions.
   - Caveat: requires more traffic and careful instrumentation for interactions.

3) Weighted blend with staged escalation (for fine-grained latency/cost tradeoffs)
   - Start with v0: 1% blend, monitor both unit economics and quality. If OK, increment to 5%, 15%, then 50%.
   - Automated stop conditions: 3 consecutive 5-minute windows of metric breaches or a single severe incident.
   - Useful for quantization or runtime kernel swaps where gradual exposure helps catch rare edge cases.

4) Canary-with-exploratory-threads (safer dynamic probing)
   - Keep main route deterministic to baseline. Send a fraction of traffic copies via shadowing to candidate stacks for offline QA metrics (no customer impact).
   - For selected queries (synthetic or high-value), return candidate results to a mirror client for human review.

Signal selection (what to watch) — recommended minimum set for LLM inference rollouts:
- Latency p95/p99 (per route and per model variant)
- Error rate (5xx/timeout/partial failures)
- Token-level cost per request (billed tokens + internal execution cost estimate)
- Quality signals: rerank loss, automated eval score (BLEU/ROUGE not sufficient), hallucination proxy (unknown-entity-rate), safety classifiers triggers
- Business KPIs: completion rate, CTA clickthrough, NPS sample (if available)
- Operational signals: queue growth, OOMs, GPU memory pressure, cold-start frequency

Quick instrumentation checklist (must-haves before any canary):
- Per-cohort tagging at the routing layer and in logs (cohort_id)
- Aggregated metric pipelines per cohort (latency, cost, error) with 1m granularity
- Alerting rules for cohort-specific thresholds (not just global)
- Synthetics: a small suite of probe prompts that cover short/long contexts, hallucination-prone inputs, edge cases
- Debug hooks: trace-id propagation, saved example buckets for failing queries

Risk thresholds and automated guardrails (suggested starting values) — conservative defaults, tune by service:
- Immediate rollback triggers (action: automatic revert to baseline):
  - Error rate relative increase > 3x baseline for 5m
  - Latency p99 increase > 2x baseline sustained over 2 consecutive 1m windows
  - Safety classifier triggers > 2x baseline (for any severity level)
- Soft stop (manual review required):
  - Cost per request (unit) increase > 30% vs baseline for 15m
  - Small but consistent degradation in a quality proxy (e.g., rerank drop > 5% for 30m)

Operational runbook snippet (who does what on an alert):
- Pager: SRE
  - Step 0: Acknowledge and add ‘canary-rollback’ tag to incident channel
  - Step 1: SRE evaluates cohort-specific dashboards (pre-built) and checks recent deploys/traffic changes
  - Step 2: If immediate rollback trigger met, flip route to baseline via console rollback; notify product/engineering and record action in incident log
- Product owner:
  - Evaluate user-facing impact; decide on communication to CS if customer-facing regression
- Engineering (model/runtime owner):
  - Investigate root cause, triage logs, run problematic samples locally against baseline and candidate

Cross-functional communications (brief ceremony template):
- On canary start: Slack announcement (#rollouts) with scope, cohort IDs, expected duration, owner and rollback contact
- Mid-canary sync (if >2hr): short async status update: metrics snapshot + notable failing samples
- On rollback: summary + learnings + immediate follow-ups assigned

Cohort orthogonalization heuristics (practical tips)
- Always prefer fewer independent variables per cohort; it simplifies attribution and reduces debug time.
- Use deterministic hashing on a stable user attribute where possible to guarantee cohort stickiness (user_id/email_hash). For anonymous routes, consider request-fingerprint with TTL.
- For short-lived sessions (e.g., chat with ephemeral ids), prefer session-based partitioning and record mapping for replay.
- Avoid overlapping cohorts across simultaneous experiments in adjacent product surfaces that share user segments (e.g., both in-app assistant and search). If unavoidable, schedule them staggered.

Blend patterns specific to inference runtimes:
- Kernel-only blends: same model weights, different runtime kernels (e.g., cuBLAS vs fused kernels). Useful for perf tuning.
- Quantization blends: baseline fp16 vs int4; expect subtle quality regressions — monitor hallucination proxies closely.
- Routing blends: same model but different routing policies (region vs cost-based). Monitor end-to-end latency and cross-region fallbacks.

Failed experiments we learned from (short notes):
- Experiment: 10% traffic to combined model+routing change (single cohort). Result: ambiguous quality drop. Lesson: split axes next time; run orthogonal matrix.
- Experiment: dynamic allocation using a naive reward signal (CTR only). Result: allocation pushed traffic to a lower-latency but lower-quality variant. Lesson: composite reward required (quality + cost + safety).

Open questions / items for follow-up:
- Define a canonical quality composite score (weighted) for dynamic allocation experiments. Who owns weights? Product + metrics?
- What is an acceptable maximum cohort size for high-visibility customer routes? (Ops + sales need input)
- How to expose canary cohort discovery to CS so they can triage customer tickets generated during experiments?

Next steps (short roadmap):
1) Draft a templated console view for orthogonal canaries (cohort-level panels): owner, cohort size, top failure samples, key metrics
2) Build a small synthetic probe deck for LLM-specific failure modes (hallucination, repetition, truncation) and add to pipeline
3) Pilot orthogonal matrix on a low-risk route next week; collect post-mortem and refine guardrail thresholds
4) Design a composite reward function prototype for constrained dynamic allocation (eng + product + applied-ml)

Notes to self (random):
- Consider a ‘canary-id’ header to make downstream tracing and customer support correlation simpler.
- Keep human-review windows short and focused; too much manual review slows iteration.

References / quick links:
- Linked artifacts above (JIRA/Confluence/PR).
- Internal SRE playbooks for rollback mechanics (see CONFLUENCE:runbook/sre-rollback)

If you read this and want to try a concrete experiment, ping me and I’ll help set up the cohorts in the staging console.

End.
